title: Millions Face Deportation Without a Lawyer as Legal Aid Programs Collapse
excerpt: More than half of immigrants in removal proceedings lack legal representation, and the federal government is letting key contracts expire — putting tens of thousands of children and adults at heightened risk.
body:
• Fifty-four percent of immigrants facing deportation in the U.S. go to court without a lawyer, according to the Vera Institute of Justice.
  • Immigration courts are scheduling "mega master" hearings with 100 or more people at a time, predominantly targeting unrepresented immigrants.
  • The Trump administration is allowing a federal contract providing legal services to roughly 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children to expire, with no replacement announced.
  • States including Colorado, Massachusetts, and Washington have stepped in with their own immigrant legal defense funds, but advocates say a federal solution is needed.

When an immigrant walks into a U.S. immigration courtroom without a lawyer, the odds are stacked sharply against them. Unlike criminal courts, where defendants have a constitutional right to a public defender, immigration proceedings are classified as civil — meaning the government has no obligation to provide counsel, even when the outcome is deportation to a country the person fled.

That gap is widening. According to the Vera Institute of Justice, 54 percent of people facing removal currently lack legal representation. And recent policy shifts are making the problem worse.

"Mega Master" Hearings

Immigration courts have begun scheduling what attorneys call "mega masters" — mass hearings that pack 100 or more respondents into a single session. Previously, master calendar hearings typically handled two to three dozen people at a time.

The practice started in Chicago, Boston, and Chelmsford, Massachusetts, and is expanding to Dallas, according to NPR reporting. Immigration attorneys and the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) say the hearings disproportionately target people without lawyers.

"They're anticipating that the majority will not show up and they'll just be able to say that they completed X number of cases because they'll be in absentia orders of removal."

— Texas-based immigration attorney, speaking to NPR

When respondents miss their hearing — sometimes because their dates were rescheduled with little or no notice — judges can issue in absentia removal orders, fast-tracking deportation. Many of the people being summoned had original hearing dates scheduled for 2027, 2028, or 2029.

Children Lose Legal Lifeline

In a parallel development, the Trump administration allowed a federal contract providing legal services to unaccompanied migrant children to expire in August 2026. The contract funded a network of nearly 100 legal organizations that served roughly 20,000 children who entered the U.S. without a parent or guardian.

Under the contract, lawyers could enter government-funded shelters to present children with information about their legal rights and directly represent them in immigration proceedings. With no replacement announced, those services are in limbo.

"We have no understanding of what's going to happen to those children. We don't know if they're going to have legal representation," said Melissa Lopez, executive director of Estrella El Paso, which currently represents 243 unaccompanied children in western Texas and New Mexico.

Organizations say the government has withheld payments for more than six months, demanding detailed client information that providers say they have never previously been asked for and cannot ethically disclose. Some groups have begun laying off staff. ProBar in south Texas cut 20 percent of its workforce, and Mid-South Immigration Advocates in Memphis plans to close entirely after being owed more than $500,000.

What Legal Representation Changes

The evidence that lawyers make a difference is substantial. A randomized study by the Vera Institute, examining the Midwest Immigrant Defenders Alliance (MIDA) program in Chicago, found that legal representation produced significant positive impacts on case outcomes — regardless of which presidential administration was in power or which judge presided.

Having a lawyer significantly reduces the likelihood of deportation for detained immigrants, the study found, and the benefits held across judges with varying levels of strictness.

States Step In

With federal legal aid contracting, several states have established their own immigrant legal defense funds. Colorado created an immigration legal defense fund in 2021. Massachusetts allocated $5 million in its 2025 budget for immigration legal services. Washington appropriated funding to contract with organizations providing representation for low-income immigrants.

Advocates say these state programs are essential but insufficient to address a nationwide crisis. The Fairness to Freedom Act, backed by the National Partnership for New Americans and the Vera Institute, would establish a federal right to representation for all immigrants facing deportation — but it has not advanced in Congress.

What It Means for the Indian Community

While the mega master hearings and children's legal aid crisis primarily affect asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants, the broader erosion of due process in immigration courts touches every immigrant community. Indian nationals facing removal proceedings — whether from visa overstays, status lapses, or other issues — operate in the same court system where representation can determine whether someone stays or is deported. Community legal organizations serving South Asian immigrants, including groups like the South Asian Bar Association and SAALT, have urged members to seek legal counsel before any interaction with immigration authorities.
